speaker: Patrick Hsu
title: Arc Institute's Patrick Hsu on Building an App Store for Biology with AI
question: In experimental biology, why does the published scientific literature fail to capture how wet-lab discovery actually works?
guest: We have done a lot of biology with what is not that far from guess and check. If you look at what happens in the wet lab, the actual experiments that are happening, you're just in the arena trying stuff—trying out hypotheses and seeing what happens. The missing reasoning trace in the scientific literature is you don't know what didn't work. Everything is narrativized and written in a story of inexorable logic and vision leading to a scientific breakthrough, but everyone who makes the sausage knows that's not what actually happens most of the time. That high-fidelity reasoning trace of the true process is not written down anywhere, and that would actually be very useful for reasoning models and closing the loop. Because what actually happens is guess and check, a model with even moderate predictive value—which we don't have—would be transformative. Biology is a very pragmatic, salt-of-the-earth experimental discipline, and you see this in the culture of peer review: show me the data. You can't pontificate in your discussion section because you haven't shown any of it.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Published papers are retrospective, polished arguments rather than records of what happened, so they systematically omit most of the actual discovery process.

First, papers rationalize the path. Results are rearranged into a clean hypothesis-to-conclusion narrative, hiding the dead ends, accidents, pivots, and iterative troubleshooting that drove the work. Peter Medawar made this point in 1963 when he asked whether the scientific paper is "a fraud."

Second, negative and failed results rarely get published. Most experiments fail or are ambiguous, and that information, which shapes what researchers try next, stays in lab notebooks. Publication bias and incentives favoring novel, positive stories reinforce this.

Third, methods sections are compressed and incomplete. Success often depends on tacit knowledge: how to handle cells, reagent lots, timing, what a "good" prep looks like, and which protocol steps actually matter. This is passed on through apprenticeship, not text, and is a major contributor to irreproducibility.

Finally, the judgment itself goes unrecorded: why one experiment was chosen over another, how anomalies were interpreted, and when to abandon a line of work.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Published biology papers reconstruct messy, opportunistic exploration into tidy linear narratives. Shaped by journal conventions and peer review, authors present a clean sequence of pre-formed hypotheses and decisive tests—what François Jacob called "day science"—while erasing the "night science" of false starts, puzzling anomalies, and shifting questions that actually drove the work. Because incentives reward positive, coherent stories, most wet-lab reality disappears from print: months of assay troubleshooting, abandoned hypotheses, informative negative results, and serendipitous accidents reframed after the fact as deliberate design.

Equally absent is tacit knowledge. Methods sections compress intricate physical craft into standardized recipes, omitting the subtle visual cues, reagent batch quirks, environmental sensitivities, and hands-on heuristics passed down informally at the bench. Together, publication bias, post-hoc rationalization, and compressed protocols turn an iterative, error-prone search through biological complexity into an illusion of frictionless deduction—leaving readers with polished conclusions, but little record of the true experimental path or the unwritten know-how required to reproduce it.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The published literature records what worked, not how researchers got there. Papers are written afterward as neat, logical stories, a point Peter Medawar made when he called the scientific paper a "fraud." The real process involves false starts, troubleshooting, lucky accidents and changing hypotheses, and all of that gets edited out.

Three other forces make the gap wider. Publication bias means failed experiments and negative results rarely get published, so the large body of knowledge about what doesn't work never appears in print. Much bench skill is tacit knowledge, in the sense described by Michael Polanyi and Harry Collins: the feel for when cells look healthy, how hard to pipette, or which reagent batch behaves oddly. It passes from person to person in the lab and resists being written down, which helps explain why protocols often fail to reproduce elsewhere. Finally, page limits and career incentives push authors to compress methods sections and present results as confident and linear.

As a result, anyone learning only from papers, whether a student or an AI model, sees a biased, cleaned-up version of science. They miss the iterative, error-driven process that actually produces discoveries.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Published biology papers reconstruct discovery as a clean, linear progression from hypothesis to proof, obscuring the messy, iterative reality of the bench. In practice, wet-lab research is dominated by failed experiments, dead-end hypotheses, accidental observations, and long stretches of troubleshooting—yet publication bias and journal norms strip away these negative results and detours, leaving only the final, polished narrative. Equally important, written methods sections cannot capture the tacit, embodied craft of experimental biology. Whether a protocol succeeds often hinges on subtle, unrecorded details: how gently cells are handled, slight differences in reagent batches, ambient lab conditions, or the informal intuition a researcher develops through repetition. Figures similarly curate representative, best-case outcomes rather than the noisy biological variability encountered day to day. By presenting finished conclusions instead of the exploratory process, dead ends, and hands-on skills that produced them, the literature records what was ultimately found—and what survived peer review—rather than how discovery actually happens in the lab.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Wet-lab discovery is iterative, but a paper is usually organized around the evidence for a final claim. Researchers spend much of their time troubleshooting assays, revising hypotheses, and deciding whether an unexpected result reflects biology or a problem with the experiment. A paper may describe the controls that ultimately resolved that ambiguity while leaving out the detours that made those controls necessary.

Publication also favors clear, novel findings, so null results and abandoned approaches often stay in lab notebooks. Even a detailed methods section can miss tacit knowledge, such as how an experienced researcher recognizes an unhealthy cell culture or decides when an assay is behaving oddly. The published record can therefore explain why a conclusion deserves confidence while giving a much thinner account of how researchers figured out what to try next.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A paper usually tells you why a conclusion is warranted. It rarely tells you how the researchers came to ask that particular question or run that particular experiment. In the lab, a failed assay might reveal a flaw in the setup, an unexpected result might change the question, and a colleague might notice something that the written protocol never mentions. Researchers often work out what an observation means while they are still learning how to measure it reliably.

When they write the paper, they organize the evidence around the claim they can ultimately defend. False starts, inconclusive results, and practical judgments often drop out because of space limits, reporting conventions, and incentives to publish clear findings. The resulting account can be accurate about the evidence while making the path to discovery look far more direct and predictable than it was.
